topic.title: Leaf structure, gas exchange and the compensation point
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: The Higher half sits at the very end of the paper: Summer 2025 B1 Higher Q9 was 8 marks on leaf discs, light intensity and hydrogencarbonate indicator — a trend [1], an explanation [1], two colours [1] each and a three-statement choice [3]. Summer 2024 Higher Q7 used the indicator with three respiration experiments. Leaf structure itself is common to both tiers: March 2026 Foundation Q4 named the alveolus adaptations and then asked, unsuccessfully for most, which leaf layer carries out most gas exchange.
mustMemorise: Waxy cuticle: transparent, waterproof, a physical defence
Upper epidermis: transparent; its cell walls are a physical defence
Palisade mesophyll: tightly packed end on to the upper surface, many chloroplasts — most photosynthesis
Spongy mesophyll: loosely packed, a few chloroplasts, large surface area and air spaces — most gas exchange
Guard cells and stomata, mostly on the lower surface: gases diffuse in and out
Hydrogencarbonate indicator: high CO₂ yellow, normal CO₂ red, low CO₂ purple
Compensation point: rate of photosynthesis equals rate of respiration, so no net gas exchange
notOnThisSpec: Xylem, phloem and the veins of the leaf (B2, transport in plants)
The mechanism by which guard cells open and close stomata
Transpiration and the potometer, which are B2 topics
Light-dependent and light-independent stages of photosynthesis

sheet.howExamined: B1, 1 hour: 60 marks at Foundation, 70 at Higher, calculator allowed. Leaf structure is common to both tiers, usually a labelled diagram with layers to name [1] each and one adaptation to explain [2]-[3]. The indicator and the compensation point are Higher only and sit at the end of the paper: Summer 2025 Q9 was 8 marks. Marks come as [1] lines with tight accept lists — 'spongy mesophyll' not 'mesophyll', 'purple' not 'lilac' — and a comparison part wants comparative language about both processes. A 'choose three letters' part gives [1] each and the listing rule applies to extra letters.
traps: Not knowing which layer carries out most gas exchange (March 2026 B1 F Q4)
Writing 'mesophyll' when the scheme needs palisade or spongy
Giving a structure without its function, when the mark is for the function
Confusing the waxy cuticle with the upper epidermis
Writing 'guard cells' where the question asks how gases enter — the answer is the stomata
Food-test colours written for hydrogencarbonate indicator: brick red, blue-black, lilac (Summer 2025 B1 H Q9(c)(ii))
Yellow and purple the wrong way round — yellow is HIGH carbon dioxide
Saying respiration stops in the light
Explaining a purple tube as 'the leaf photosynthesised' without comparing it with respiration
Calling the compensation point a stop, rather than two equal rates with no net exchange
Writing more letters than a 'choose three' question asks for, which invokes the listing rule
Working out what each tube is doing and then not carrying it through to the indicator: say whether that tube gained or lost carbon dioxide, and only then give the colour (Summer 2024 B1 H Q7)

steps.decision: Name the layer first. 'The top layer' is not a name, and 'mesophyll' on its own does not separate palisade from spongy.
One reason from inside the cell. Chloroplasts hold the chlorophyll, so more chloroplasts means more light absorbed.

steps.working: The cells are tightly packed, end on, just under the upper surface, so they receive the most light.
steps.decision: The second reason is about position, not contents. Two reasons of the same kind would usually earn one mark, not two.

options: Because the two marks are for two different adaptations
Because the examiner likes long answers
Because chloroplasts move towards the light
whyMenu.explain: A scheme asking for two reasons is listening for two different ideas: what the cells contain, and where they are.

steps.working: Most gas exchange: the spongy mesophyll.
steps.decision: This is the layer March 2026's candidates could not name. It is the lower of the two mesophyll layers.

steps.working: Its cells are loosely arranged with large air spaces between them.
steps.decision: Name the structural feature. 'Spongy' is a description, not an explanation.

steps.working: That gives a large surface area and lets gases diffuse freely through the leaf to and from the stomata.
steps.decision: Finish with the function: surface area plus diffusion. Both words appear in the specification's own wording for this layer.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) The palisade mesophyll: it contains many chloroplasts, and it is tightly packed end on just below the upper surface so it receives the most light. (b) The spongy mesophyll: its cells are loosely arranged with large air spaces between them, giving a large surface area and letting gases diffuse through the leaf.

twin.stem: Name the layer of the leaf that reduces water loss, and explain how.

accepted: the waxy cuticle, because it is waterproof so water cannot evaporate through the upper surface

steps.decision: One word. The listing rule means writing 'purple or red' scores nothing, so commit.

steps.working: In bright light the leaf photosynthesises faster than it respires.
steps.decision: Start with the comparison of the two rates. Saying only 'it photosynthesises' misses that respiration is happening too.

options: Because the net change is what the indicator measures
Because respiration stops in the light
Because purple is the photosynthesis colour
whyMenu.explain: Respiration never stops. The indicator responds to the difference between the two rates.

steps.working: So carbon dioxide is used up faster than it is produced, and the concentration in the tube falls.
steps.decision: Say which gas and which way. This is the link between the biology and the colour.

steps.working: Low carbon dioxide turns hydrogencarbonate indicator purple.
steps.decision: Close the loop by naming the rule you used. The scheme's third point is usually this statement.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Purple. (b) In bright light photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so carbon dioxide is used up faster than it is produced and its concentration in the tube falls; low carbon dioxide turns the indicator purple.

twin.stem: The same leaf is then wrapped in foil and left for two hours. State the colour of the indicator and explain it.

accepted: yellow, because in the dark only respiration happens so carbon dioxide is added and a high carbon dioxide level turns the indicator yellow

workedExamples.stem:
A leaf in a sealed tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator is placed in dim light. After two hours the indicator is still red.
Explain fully what this shows about the leaf. [4]

figure.alt: A graph of rate against light intensity with the rate of respiration roughly constant and the rate of photosynthesis rising, crossing at a marked compensation point.

steps.working: Red means the carbon dioxide concentration has not changed.
steps.decision: Translate the colour into a quantity before saying anything biological. Red is the starting colour, so nothing has been added or removed overall.

steps.working: The leaf is both respiring and photosynthesising.
steps.decision: Say that both are happening. A candidate who writes 'nothing is happening' has described the observation, not explained it.

steps.working: Photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates.
steps.decision: This is the definition, and it is the mark that most often goes missing. Equal rates — not 'the same amount of light'.

steps.working: So there is no net gas exchange: the leaf is at its compensation point.
steps.decision: Finish with the term and the phrase. 'No net gas exchange' and 'compensation point' are both on the scheme.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Red means the carbon dioxide concentration is unchanged. The leaf is respiring and photosynthesising at the same time, and at this light intensity photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates, so there is no net gas exchange — the leaf is at its compensation point.

accepted: the light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates, so there is no net gas exchange

items.stem: In which layer of the leaf does most gas exchange take place?

options.feedback: Its loosely arranged cells and large air spaces give the surface area and the route for diffusion.
The palisade layer is tightly packed, with little space between the cells — that suits light absorption, not gas exchange. March 2026 examiners reported few candidates identifying the right layer.
The upper epidermis is a protective transparent layer with almost no stomata in it.
The cuticle is waterproof, which is the opposite of a gas-exchange surface.

items.stem: Why does the palisade mesophyll contain the most chloroplasts?
items.skill: Match a layer to its adaptation

options.text: It is nearest the upper surface, so it receives the most light
options.feedback: Position plus contents: near the top, packed end on, and full of chloroplasts.

options.text: It has the largest air spaces
options.feedback: Large air spaces are the spongy mesophyll's feature, and they are for gas exchange.
The waxy cuticle is the waterproof one.
Stomata are in the epidermis, mostly the lower one.

items.stem: A leaf is sealed in hydrogencarbonate indicator and kept in the dark. What colour does the indicator turn?

options.feedback: Dark means respiration only, so carbon dioxide is added, and high carbon dioxide is yellow.
Purple is low carbon dioxide, which happens in bright light when photosynthesis wins.
Brick red is the positive Benedict's result and belongs to food tests. Summer 2025 examiners recorded food-test colours being written here.
Blue-black is iodine on starch. The indicator has only three colours: yellow, red and purple.

items.stem: The hydrogencarbonate indicator in a sealed tube turns purple. What does this show?
items.skill: Read a colour back to a process

options.text: The carbon dioxide level has fallen, so photosynthesis was faster than respiration
options.feedback: Purple means low carbon dioxide, and the only thing that removes it is photosynthesis outpacing respiration.

options.text: The carbon dioxide level has risen
options.feedback: Rising carbon dioxide turns the indicator yellow, not purple.
Respiration never stops. Photosynthesis is simply using carbon dioxide faster than respiration produces it.
A dead leaf would do neither, and the indicator would stay red.

options.text: The light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration happen at equal rates, so there is no net gas exchange
options.feedback: Equal rates, no net exchange — both halves are needed for a two-mark definition.

options.text: The point at which photosynthesis stops
options.feedback: Both processes are running at full speed; they simply cancel out.

options.text: The maximum rate of photosynthesis a plant can reach
options.feedback: That would be a plateau on a limiting-factor graph, not the compensation point.

options.text: The light intensity at which a leaf begins to lose water
options.feedback: Nothing about the compensation point is about water. It is about gas exchange.

items.stem: A tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator with no leaf in it is set up beside the others. Why?
items.skill: Identify the purpose of a control

options.text: To show that any colour change in the other tubes was caused by the leaf
options.feedback: A control changes only the thing being tested. If the empty tube stays red, temperature and light alone did not move the colour.

options.text: To make the experiment more reliable
options.feedback: Reliability comes from repeating. A control is about showing the cause, not about repeating.

options.text: To keep the carbon dioxide level steady in the room
options.feedback: A sealed tube has no effect on the room. It is there for comparison.
It is a comparison, not part of the apparatus.

items.stem: Which feature of the leaf is described as transparent AND waterproof?
items.skill: Separate the cuticle from the epidermis

options.feedback: Transparent so light gets through, waterproof so less water is lost, and a physical defence.
The epidermis is transparent and its cell walls are a physical defence, but the waterproofing is the waxy cuticle on top of it.
Guard cells open and close the stomata. They are not a waterproof layer.
The spongy layer is where gases move; it is neither transparent nor waterproof.

context.setting: A question about why a leaf is shaped the way it is

figures.alt: A labelled cross-section through a mesophytic leaf showing the waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air spaces, lower epidermis, guard cells and stoma.

parts.stem: Explain why the upper epidermis and the waxy cuticle are transparent.

accepted: so that light can pass through them to reach the palisade cells below

scheme.for: so light can pass through them
and reach the chloroplasts in the palisade mesophyll below, for photosynthesis

hints: Say where the light is going, not just that it gets through.
parts.workedSolution: Being transparent lets light pass straight through, so it reaches the chloroplasts in the palisade mesophyll underneath and can be used for photosynthesis.

parts.stem: Explain why the waxy cuticle is also an advantage to the plant even though it does not photosynthesise.

accepted: it is waterproof so it reduces water loss, and it is a physical defence

scheme.for: it is waterproof, so it reduces water loss from the leaf
it acts as a physical defence / barrier

hints: The spec gives the cuticle three properties: transparent, waterproof and a physical defence.
parts.workedSolution: The cuticle is waterproof, so less water evaporates from the leaf surface, and it acts as a physical defence against damage and infection.

context.setting: A question about how carbon dioxide reaches a palisade cell

figures.alt: A labelled cross-section through a mesophytic leaf showing the waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis. The opening in the lower surface, with the two cells around it, is marked A and is not named.

parts.stem: Name the structures through which carbon dioxide enters the leaf.

accepted: stomata
stoma

scheme.for: stomata

hints: The guard cells control the pores; the pores themselves have their own name.
parts.workedSolution: The stomata.

commonErrors.feedback: The guard cells open and close the pore. The pore itself is the stoma, and gases pass through it.

parts.stem: Explain how carbon dioxide reaches a palisade cell after entering the leaf.

accepted: it diffuses through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll, down a concentration gradient, because photosynthesis keeps the concentration inside the cells low

scheme.for: it diffuses through the intercellular air spaces of the spongy mesophyll
from a higher concentration outside to a lower concentration inside the cells
photosynthesis uses the carbon dioxide, keeping the concentration low and the gradient going

hints: Three marks: the route, the direction, and why the direction keeps working.
parts.workedSolution: Carbon dioxide diffuses through the intercellular air spaces of the spongy mesophyll and into the cells. It moves from the higher concentration in the air spaces to the lower concentration inside the cells, and because photosynthesis keeps using it up, that concentration gradient is maintained.

commonErrors.feedback: Gases move into a leaf by diffusion, down a concentration gradient. No energy is used.

parts.stem: Complete the table.

scheme.for: yellow
red
purple

hints: Three colours in order of falling carbon dioxide: yellow, red, purple.
None of the food-test colours appears here.
parts.workedSolution: High carbon dioxide: yellow. Normal: red. Low: purple.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are food-test colours from section 1.3. The indicator has only yellow, red and purple — Summer 2025 examiners saw exactly this mix-up.
The order is reversed. High carbon dioxide turns it yellow; removing carbon dioxide takes it towards purple.

parts.stem:
A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator and left in a dark cupboard overnight.
State the colour of the indicator the next morning.

accepted: yellow

scheme.for: yellow
scheme.examinerNote: One colour only; two colours invoke the listing rule.

hints: What is the leaf doing in the dark, and what does that do to the carbon dioxide?
parts.workedSolution: Yellow.

parts.stem: Explain your answer.

accepted: in the dark there is no photosynthesis, so only respiration happens and carbon dioxide is released, raising the concentration, and high carbon dioxide turns the indicator yellow

scheme.for: in the dark the leaf cannot photosynthesise
but it continues to respire, releasing carbon dioxide
so the carbon dioxide concentration rises, and a high level turns the indicator yellow

hints: Three links: no photosynthesis, respiration continues, carbon dioxide rises.
parts.workedSolution: Without light the leaf cannot photosynthesise, but it goes on respiring, which releases carbon dioxide into the sealed tube. The carbon dioxide concentration therefore rises, and a high carbon dioxide level turns hydrogencarbonate indicator yellow.

commonErrors.feedback: Respiration happens all the time, day and night. What stops in the dark is photosynthesis.

context.setting: A definition question at the start of a Higher gas-exchange question

figures.alt: A graph of rate against light intensity with the rate of respiration roughly constant and the rate of photosynthesis rising, crossing at a marked compensation point.

parts.stem: Define the compensation point.

accepted: the light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates, so there is no net gas exchange

scheme.for: photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates
so there is no net gas exchange
accept: no overall exchange of gases with the surroundings

hints: Two ideas: equal rates, and the consequence for gas exchange.
The word 'net' matters — both processes are still running.
parts.workedSolution: The compensation point is the light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis is exactly equal to the rate of respiration, so there is no net gas exchange between the plant and its surroundings.

commonErrors.feedback: Both processes are running at full speed; they cancel out. Say 'equal rates' and 'no net gas exchange'.

parts.stem: Explain why a plant kept permanently at its compensation point would not grow.

accepted: all the glucose made by photosynthesis is used up by respiration, so there is none left for growth

scheme.for: photosynthesis makes only as much glucose as respiration uses
so there is no surplus left for growth or storage

hints: Think about what the glucose is for, not just about the gases.
parts.workedSolution: At the compensation point photosynthesis makes exactly as much glucose as respiration breaks down, so there is no surplus left over to build new cells or to store as starch, and the plant cannot grow.

context.setting: Four sealed tubes of indicator left for two hours

figures.alt: Four sealed test tubes of hydrogencarbonate indicator: tube A with no leaf stays red, a leaf in the dark turns yellow, a leaf in dim light stays red, and a leaf in bright light turns purple.

parts.stem:
Tube A contains indicator but no leaf.
Explain why tube A is needed.

accepted: it is a control, and it shows that any colour change in the other tubes was caused by the leaf

scheme.for: it is a control
it shows that any colour change in the other tubes is caused by the leaf and not by the light or the temperature

hints: A control differs from the others in exactly one way.
parts.workedSolution: Tube A is the control. Everything about it is the same except that it holds no leaf, so if it stays red while the others change, the change must have been caused by the leaf rather than by the light or the temperature.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeats give reliability. A control shows what caused the change.

parts.stem: Suggest why the indicator in tube C is still red after two hours.

accepted: the leaf is at its compensation point, so photosynthesis and respiration are at equal rates and there is no net gas exchange

scheme.for: photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates / the leaf is at its compensation point
so there is no net change in the carbon dioxide concentration and the colour does not change

hints: Tube C is in dim light, so neither process has the upper hand.
parts.workedSolution: In dim light the leaf is at its compensation point: it photosynthesises and respires at equal rates, so the carbon dioxide it releases is used up as fast as it is made. There is no net change in carbon dioxide, so the indicator stays red.

commonErrors.feedback: Both processes are running — they cancel. That is the compensation point, and it is worth naming.

context.setting: A desert plant with a very thick cuticle and sunken stomata

parts.stem:
A desert plant has a much thicker waxy cuticle than a typical mesophytic leaf, and far fewer stomata.
Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of these features for the plant.

accepted: less water is lost, but less carbon dioxide can enter so the rate of photosynthesis is lower

scheme.for: advantage: less water is lost from the leaf
disadvantage: less carbon dioxide can diffuse in, so the rate of photosynthesis is lower

hints: Every adaptation costs something. The stomata are the way in for carbon dioxide as well as the way out for water.
parts.workedSolution: The thick cuticle and the small number of stomata mean much less water is lost by the leaf, which matters in a desert. The cost is that less carbon dioxide can diffuse into the leaf, so the rate of photosynthesis is lower.

context.setting: A comparison of a flat broad leaf with a rolled-up one

parts.stem: Explain why a mesophytic leaf is broad and thin.

accepted: a broad leaf has a large surface area to absorb light, and a thin leaf gives a short diffusion distance for gases

scheme.for: broad gives a large surface area
so more light can be absorbed for photosynthesis
thin gives a short diffusion distance, so gases reach the mesophyll cells quickly

hints: Two features, two reasons: broad for one thing, thin for another.
parts.workedSolution: Being broad gives the leaf a large surface area, so it can absorb more light for photosynthesis. Being thin means gases have only a short distance to diffuse between the stomata and the mesophyll cells, so carbon dioxide reaches the cells quickly.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the broadness has been explained. The thinness is a separate adaptation, for a short diffusion distance.

context.setting: A list of lettered statements about a leaf in a sealed tube in the dark

parts.stem:
A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator and moved from bright light into the dark. After two hours the indicator has turned yellow.
Choose the **three** statements that explain this.

A  photosynthesis has stopped
B  respiration has stopped
C  respiration is still taking place
D  oxygen is being released overall
E  carbon dioxide is being released overall
F  the carbon dioxide concentration in the tube has fallen
G  the carbon dioxide concentration in the tube has risen

options.feedback: Correct: without light there is no photosynthesis.
Respiration never stops. It is photosynthesis that stops in the dark.
Correct: the leaf goes on respiring day and night.
Oxygen is being used up by respiration, not released — that would need photosynthesis.
Correct: respiration releases carbon dioxide, and nothing is using it.
A falling carbon dioxide level would turn the indicator purple. Yellow means it has risen.
This is true, but the question asks for three statements and A, C and E are the three that explain the change; G restates the colour rather than explaining it.

scheme.for: A, C and E in any order — [1] each
scheme.examinerNote: More than three letters invokes the listing rule (Summer 2025 B1 H Q9(c)(i) used the same format).

hints: Three statements, so three letters and no more.
Ask what has changed (the light), what has not (respiration) and what that does to the carbon dioxide.
parts.workedSolution: A: in the dark there is no light, so photosynthesis has stopped. C: respiration continues all the time. E: with respiration running and photosynthesis stopped, carbon dioxide is released overall, which is what turns the indicator yellow.

commonErrors.feedback: B says respiration has stopped, which is never true of a living leaf. It is photosynthesis that needs the light.

context.setting: A graph of the net carbon dioxide exchange of a leaf through 24 hours

parts.stem: Describe the net gas exchange of a leaf at three times of day: at midnight, at dawn and at midday.

accepted: midnight: carbon dioxide released and oxygen taken in; dawn: no net exchange; midday: carbon dioxide taken in and oxygen released

scheme.for: midnight: respiration only, so carbon dioxide is released and oxygen taken in
dawn: photosynthesis and respiration at equal rates, so no net gas exchange (compensation point)
midday: photosynthesis faster than respiration, so carbon dioxide is taken in and oxygen released

hints: Three times, three answers — and each one is about the net result, not about which process is running.
parts.workedSolution: At midnight the leaf only respires, so it releases carbon dioxide and takes in oxygen. At dawn the light intensity reaches the compensation point, photosynthesis and respiration run at equal rates and there is no net gas exchange. At midday photosynthesis is much faster than respiration, so the leaf takes carbon dioxide in and releases oxygen.

commonErrors.feedback: Respiration continues at midday too. What you measure is the difference between the two, which is why 'net' is in the question.

parts.stem: Explain why a plant in a sealed greenhouse would die if the light were left off for several weeks.

accepted: it could not photosynthesise so it would make no glucose, but it would go on respiring and use up its stores

scheme.for: with no light it cannot photosynthesise, so it makes no glucose
it continues to respire, so it uses up its stored starch and eventually has no energy source

hints: One process stops; the other does not.
parts.workedSolution: Without light the plant cannot photosynthesise, so it makes no new glucose. It goes on respiring day and night, using up the starch it had stored, and once those stores are gone it has no source of energy.

context.setting: An electron micrograph of a single stoma with a scale bar

figures.alt: Scanning electron micrograph of a single open stoma on a leaf surface, the pore framed by two sausage-shaped cells, with a ten micrometre scale bar printed along the bottom
figures.credit: Charles Tschirhart, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
figures.prompt: Use the scale bar to estimate how long the pore is.

parts.stem: Name the two cells on either side of the pore.

accepted: guard cells

scheme.for: guard cells

parts.workedSolution: Guard cells.

parts.stem:
On the micrograph the scale bar represents 10 µm and is 90 mm long as printed. The pore measures 63 mm as printed.
Calculate the real length of the pore in µm.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: 90 mm represents 10 µm, so 1 mm represents 10 ÷ 90 µm
7 (µm)
scheme.examinerNote: Units needed. Correct answer with working is worth [3].

hints: Work out what one millimetre on the print represents first.
The answer must be smaller than 10 µm, because the pore is shorter than the scale bar.
parts.workedSolution: The 90 mm bar stands for 10 µm, so each printed millimetre stands for 10 ÷ 90 µm. The pore is 63 mm long on the print, so its real length is 63 × 10 ÷ 90 = 7 µm.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the wrong way round: 90 ÷ 63 × 10. The pore is shorter than the scale bar, so its length must be less than 10 µm.

questions.solutionProgram: scale: 90 mm = 10 um, so 1 mm = 10/90 um; pore 63 mm -> 63 * 10 / 90 = 7 um; inverted variant 90/63*10 = 14.29

context.setting: Leaf discs floating in a sealed tube of indicator under a lamp that is moved away in stages

figures.alt: Four sealed test tubes of hydrogencarbonate indicator: A, a control with no leaf; B, a leaf wrapped in foil; C, a leaf with one lamp far off; D, a leaf with a lamp close.

parts.stem: Name the layer of a leaf in which most gas exchange takes place.

accepted: spongy mesophyll

scheme.for: spongy mesophyll

parts.workedSolution: The spongy mesophyll.

commonErrors.feedback: The palisade layer is packed tightly for light absorption. Gas exchange happens where the air spaces are, in the spongy mesophyll.

parts.stem: State the colour of the indicator in tube D, which held a leaf in bright light.

accepted: purple

scheme.for: purple

parts.workedSolution: Purple.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are food-test colours. The indicator goes purple when carbon dioxide is low.

parts.stem: Explain the colour in tube D.

accepted: photosynthesis was faster than respiration so carbon dioxide was used up faster than it was made, the concentration fell, and low carbon dioxide turns the indicator purple

scheme.for: the leaf photosynthesised
faster than it respired
accept: photosynthesis was going faster than respiration

scheme.for: so carbon dioxide was removed from the tube, and a low carbon dioxide level turns the indicator purple

hints: Name both processes and compare their rates — that comparison is a mark on its own.
parts.workedSolution: In bright light the leaf photosynthesised faster than it respired, so carbon dioxide was used up faster than respiration produced it. The carbon dioxide concentration in the sealed tube fell, and a low carbon dioxide level turns hydrogencarbonate indicator purple.

commonErrors.feedback: The answer says photosynthesis happened but never compares it with respiration, and the comparison is where the second mark is. CCEA's schemes ask for comparative language about both things.

parts.stem: The lamp beside tube D is moved further away in stages. Explain what will happen to the colour of the indicator, and name the point at which it stops changing.

accepted: as the light intensity falls photosynthesis slows, so the indicator moves back from purple towards red, and it stops changing at the compensation point where the two rates are equal

scheme.for: as the light intensity falls the rate of photosynthesis falls
so less carbon dioxide is removed and the indicator returns from purple towards red
it stops changing at the compensation point, where photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates

hints: Follow the carbon dioxide: less photosynthesis means less of it removed.
There is a name for the light intensity where the two rates balance.
parts.workedSolution: Moving the lamp away lowers the light intensity, so the rate of photosynthesis falls and less carbon dioxide is removed from the tube. The carbon dioxide concentration rises back towards normal and the indicator changes from purple back towards red. It stops changing at the compensation point, where the rate of photosynthesis is exactly equal to the rate of respiration and there is no net gas exchange.

context.setting: A leaf cross-section printed beside a photograph of the same leaf

figures.alt: A cross-section through a mesophytic leaf. The waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, lower epidermis and the guard cells and stoma are labelled; the two middle layers are marked C and D and are not named.

Light micrograph of a stained leaf cross-section cut through the midrib: a single row of tall, column-shaped cells lies just under the upper surface on each side, rounded cells with gaps between them fill the lower half, and a vascular bundle sits in the centre of the midrib
figures.prompt: Which layer in the photograph matches the palisade mesophyll in the diagram?

parts.stem:
The two middle layers of the leaf are marked **C** and **D** in the diagram.
Name these two layers, and describe one difference between them.

accepted: palisade mesophyll and spongy mesophyll; the palisade cells are tightly packed with many chloroplasts while the spongy cells are loosely packed with air spaces and few chloroplasts

scheme.for: palisade mesophyll
spongy mesophyll
one difference, stated comparatively: palisade cells are tightly packed with many chloroplasts, spongy cells are loosely packed with air spaces and few chloroplasts
scheme.examinerNote: A comparison must describe both layers.

hints: A difference needs both sides of it — say what each layer is like.
parts.workedSolution: The palisade mesophyll and the spongy mesophyll. The palisade cells are tightly packed and contain many chloroplasts, while the spongy cells are loosely packed with large air spaces between them and contain only a few chloroplasts.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one layer has been described. CCEA's schemes ask for comparisons that mention both things being compared.

parts.stem: Explain how the structure of the spongy mesophyll suits it for gas exchange.

accepted: its cells are loosely arranged with large air spaces, giving a large surface area and letting gases diffuse freely through the leaf

scheme.for: the cells are loosely arranged with large intercellular air spaces
giving a large surface area for gas exchange
so gases can diffuse freely through the leaf to and from the stomata

hints: Three marks: the structure, the surface area it creates, and what that allows.
parts.workedSolution: The spongy mesophyll cells are loosely arranged with large intercellular air spaces between them. That gives a large surface area in contact with air, and lets carbon dioxide and oxygen diffuse freely through the leaf between the stomata and the cells.

parts.stem: Explain why most stomata are found on the lower surface of a leaf.

accepted: the lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water is lost by evaporation through the open stomata

scheme.for: the lower surface is shaded from direct sunlight, so it is cooler
so less water evaporates and is lost through the stomata

hints: Stomata have to be open for gas exchange, and that also lets water out.
parts.workedSolution: The lower surface is shaded from direct sunlight, so it stays cooler than the upper surface. Less water therefore evaporates from the leaf while the stomata are open for gas exchange.

context.setting: A gardener asking why her greenhouse plants grow at night as well as in the day

parts.stem:
A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator. Describe and explain the colour of the indicator when the leaf is kept in bright light, in dim light and in the dark.
Use the ideas of photosynthesis, respiration and the compensation point in your answer.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at the normal carbon dioxide level of the air
in bright light the indicator turns purple
because photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so carbon dioxide is removed
in the dark the indicator turns yellow
because there is no photosynthesis but respiration continues, releasing carbon dioxide
in dim light the indicator stays red
because photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates, the compensation point, so there is no net gas exchange

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Three light levels, and for each one a colour and a reason — that is six of the seven points.
Use the word 'net', and name the compensation point: both appear in the indicative content.
parts.workedSolution: Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red when the carbon dioxide level is the normal level found in air. In bright light the indicator turns purple, because the leaf photosynthesises faster than it respires and so removes carbon dioxide from the tube. In the dark the indicator turns yellow, because there is no light for photosynthesis but the leaf goes on respiring, releasing carbon dioxide. In dim light the indicator stays red: the rate of photosynthesis is exactly equal to the rate of respiration, which is the compensation point, so there is no net gas exchange and the carbon dioxide level does not change.

commonErrors.feedback: Food-test colours have been used. Summer 2025 examiners reported exactly this on the Higher paper. The indicator has three colours only: yellow, red and purple.

findTheMistake.stem:
Méabh is asked: 'A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator and left in bright light. State the colour of the indicator and explain your answer. [4]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The leaf is photosynthesising in the light.
So the carbon dioxide level in the tube goes down.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The biology is right from line 2 onwards, but the colour is from the wrong topic: brick red is the positive Benedict's result for reducing sugar. Hydrogencarbonate indicator has only three colours — yellow, red and purple — and a fall in carbon dioxide takes it to purple.
correction: The leaf photosynthesises faster than it respires in bright light.
So carbon dioxide is used up faster than it is produced.
A low carbon dioxide level turns hydrogencarbonate indicator purple.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the four marks: the reasoning about carbon dioxide stands on its own. What goes is the colour mark, and with it the final mark that ties the colour to the carbon dioxide level. Summer 2025's examiners recorded a full range of wrong colours here, food-test colours among them. It is also worth adding the comparison in line 2 — photosynthesis faster than respiration, not simply photosynthesis happening.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciarán is asked: 'The indicator around a leaf in dim light is still red after two hours. Explain what this shows. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The indicator has not changed colour.
This is because the leaf is not doing anything.
Photosynthesis and respiration have both stopped.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: No change in colour means no change in the carbon dioxide concentration, which is not the same as nothing happening. At the compensation point both processes are running at full speed: every molecule of carbon dioxide respiration releases is taken straight back by photosynthesis, so nothing crosses the leaf surface overall.
correction: The carbon dioxide concentration has not changed.
The leaf is both photosynthesising and respiring, at equal rates.
So there is no net gas exchange: the leaf is at its compensation point.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first line earns its mark — reading the colour as 'no change in carbon dioxide' is exactly right, and many answers never get that far. The two lost marks are the two ideas that turn an observation into an explanation: equal rates, and no *net* exchange. Learn 'net' as the load-bearing word: it is the difference between 'nothing is happening' and 'two things are cancelling out'.

prompts.prompt: Name the six layers of a mesophytic leaf from the top down.
prompts.answer: Waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll (with intercellular air spaces), lower epidermis, and the guard cells with their stomata.

prompts.prompt: Give two adaptations of the palisade mesophyll and say what each is for.
prompts.answer: Many chloroplasts, to absorb the light; tightly packed end on just under the upper surface, so it receives the most light.

prompts.prompt: Which layer of the leaf does most gas exchange take place in, and why?
prompts.answer: The spongy mesophyll: its cells are loosely arranged with large air spaces, giving a large surface area and letting gases diffuse through the leaf.

prompts.prompt: Give three properties of the waxy cuticle.
prompts.answer: Transparent so light passes through; waterproof so water loss is reduced; a physical defence.

prompts.prompt: Hydrogencarbonate indicator: high CO₂ ___ , normal CO₂ ___ , low CO₂ ___ .
A leaf in a sealed tube of indicator turns it yellow. What was happening?
prompts.answer: Only respiration: no photosynthesis, so carbon dioxide was released and its concentration rose.
The light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates, so there is no net gas exchange.

prompts.prompt: Why is a control tube with no leaf set up alongside the others?
prompts.answer: To show that any colour change in the other tubes was caused by the leaf and not by the light or the temperature.

prompts.prompt: Does respiration stop in the light?
prompts.answer: No. A plant respires all the time. In bright light photosynthesis is simply faster, so the net exchange is carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.

prompts.prompt: A plant is kept exactly at its compensation point for a week. Why does it not grow?
prompts.answer: Photosynthesis makes only as much glucose as respiration uses, so there is no surplus for growth or storage.
